strengths: Well-motivated and timely problem: automated, scalable reconstruction of cluster surface mass density for the 10^13.5-14 solar-mass regime that upcoming wide-field surveys will populate in large numbers, where expert-guided tools (Lenstool, WSLAP+) are impractical.

Two complementary contributions: (1) DARKCLUSTERS-15K, a large benchmark of 15,000 simulated clusters with paired mass and photometry maps spanning two simulation frameworks (IllustrisTNG, SIMBA) and multiple lens redshifts, with the generation pipeline described in reproducible detail in the appendix; (2) a physics-guided diffusion posterior sampler (photometry-conditioned DAPS prior + explicit strong/weak-lensing likelihood terms) that is fully automatic and runs in minutes.

The method design is sensible and clearly factored: physically well-defined lensing observables enter the likelihood (lens-equation geometric loss, noisy-shear loss with critical-density rescaling), while the data-driven photometry-mass relation is captured by the learned conditional prior, avoiding the rigid 1:1 light-traces-mass assumption. Appendix C quantitatively motivates this design (mass-light PCC of only ~0.58-0.65 in the dataset).

Reasonably thorough empirical validation: ablation over input components (photometry vs. SL vs. WL), quantitative comparisons against re-implemented Napier et al. and a UNet baseline on both in-distribution (TNG) and out-of-distribution (SIMBA, other redshifts) test sets, an uncertainty calibration analysis (R^2 = 0.99 between predicted STD and RMSE), and a real-data demonstration on MACS 1206 that qualitatively matches expert Lenstool reconstructions.

Strong commitment to reproducibility: code and dataset release, detailed dataset construction (particle processing, HST filter response curves, ICL modeling, noise models), and full inference hyperparameters in the appendix.
weaknesses: Sim-to-real gap is not quantitatively addressed. All quantitative results are on simulated data drawn from the same simulations used for training; the single real demonstration (MACS 1206, Fig. 6) is qualitative only, with no quantitative agreement metric against the Caminha et al. reconstruction. Given that the headline claims concern real survey data, stronger real-data evidence (e.g., additional clusters, weak-lensing shear catalogs) would materially strengthen the case.

The claim of being 'fully automatic' is partially undermined in practice: the method assumes strong-lensing multiple-image systems with source redshifts are already identified (for MACS 1206 these come from prior expert work by Caminha et al.), and inference hyperparameters (loss weights lambda_k, DAPS parameters) were hand-tuned via parameter sweeps (Appendix B). Identifying multiply imaged systems is itself a substantial expert bottleneck in cluster lensing.

Baseline comparison is somewhat unbalanced: neither the Napier et al. re-implementation nor the UNet baseline uses gravitational-lensing observables, while the proposed method consumes both lensing and photometry. A fairer comparison (e.g., a photometry-only ablation of the full pipeline, or a lensing-informed classical method) would isolate the benefit of the diffusion prior from the benefit of additional data. WSLAP+ and MARS are excluded for lack of public code.

Statistical rigor of the evaluation is modest: quantitative results cover 100 clusters drawn from only 20 underlying TNG halos (25 views each), so effective sample size is small and clusters are not independent; uncertainty calibration is summarized by a single pooled R^2 over 20 posterior samples rather than proper coverage tests; no error bars or significance tests are reported for Table 2.

Several likelihood components are heuristic rather than 'principled' as claimed: RBF interpolation of sparse shear to a dense map, independently weighted squared losses (Eq. 10), and a Sérsic-source photometric loss; the effect of these choices on posterior calibration is not analyzed.

The diffusion prior is trained only at z_L = 0.5 from IllustrisTNG; generalization to other redshifts and SIMBA is shown empirically, but the appendix discussion of how/why the prior transfers is thin, and domain-shift effects on the reported uncertainty estimates are not examined.

Minor clarity issues: Eq. 13 notation is inconsistent with the surrounding text, and the 'first fully automatic framework' claim could be more carefully qualified against prior score-based weak-lensing work (e.g., Remy et al., Boruah et al.) that the paper positions itself against only at a coarser scale.

strengths: DarkClusters-15K is a genuine contribution: 15,000 paired mass/photometry cluster maps at sub-arcsecond resolution from two independent simulation frameworks (IllustrisTNG and SIMBA), with released generation code. It is plausibly the largest benchmark of its kind and enables reproducible comparison of cluster mass-mapping methods.

The paper addresses a timely and well-motivated problem: automated, scalable, non-parametric cluster mass reconstruction for upcoming wide-field surveys where expert-tuned tools (Lenstool, WSLAP+) will not scale.

The framing is principled: a photometry-conditioned diffusion prior combined with explicit weak- and strong-lensing forward models within a DAPS posterior-sampling scheme, yielding posterior samples and per-pixel uncertainties rather than point estimates.

Useful ablations (Fig. 4) that disentangle the contribution of photometry, strong lensing, and weak lensing, and evaluation of cross-redshift (z=0.2, 0.5, 1.0) and cross-simulation (SIMBA) generalization despite training only on TNG at z=0.5.
Application to the real MACS 1206 cluster, showing qualitative agreement with an expert-tuned Lenstool reconstruction in minutes without manual tuning, is a meaningful sanity check beyond simulation.
Appendix C quantifying how far the light-traces-mass assumption holds (PCC 0.58-0.65) directly supports the paper's core claim that flexible mass-light modeling is needed.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited: the core inference machinery (DAPS, InverseBench, DDPM++/EDM training) is adopted nearly off-the-shelf, and the main additions—a photometry-conditioned prior and a heuristic photometric Sérsic-based loss (Eq. 13)—are engineering contributions. The claimed 'principled factorization' is blurred because photometry enters both the prior conditioning and the likelihood term.

The uncertainty-calibration evidence is weak: R²=0.99 between predicted posterior std and sample RMSE (Fig. 3) is a correlation, not calibration. Proper calibration (e.g., z-score statistics, coverage of credible intervals) is not reported, so the headline claim of 'well-calibrated uncertainties' is not adequately supported.

Effective dataset diversity is much smaller than the 15K headline: only 500 TNG and 60 SIMBA distinct 3D clusters, each contributing 25 correlated projections. The 25 views of one cluster are highly dependent, which weakens both training diversity and the statistical strength of the 3,000-sample test sets.

Baseline comparisons are limited and arguably uneven: Napier et al. [37] uses only photometry (no lensing observables) and the UNet baseline is likewise photometry-only, so the comparison partly measures input information rather than method quality. No quantitative comparison on simulations against MARS or expert tools; MARS is dismissed for lack of public code, but the authors' own re-implementation of Napier et al. shows this is feasible.

Real-data evaluation (MACS 1206) is purely qualitative; no quantitative agreement metric (e.g., projected mass within aperture) is reported, and there is no discussion of the substantial domain gap (PSF, noise, source extraction, masks) between simulated HST-like photometry and real observations.

The weak-lensing forward model relies on RBF interpolation of extremely noisy, sparse shear measurements (SNR 0.01-0.1); the potential impact of this smoothing on the likelihood gradients and posterior fidelity is not analyzed, and the mapping between the two noise regimes (σ²w = 0.03 vs 0.3) and realistic observational scenarios remains vague.

Several quantitative claims lack rigor: no statistical significance tests on the Table 2 improvements, no explicit runtime numbers substantiating the 'minutes vs hours' claim, and hyperparameters were tuned on a validation split without sensitivity analysis reported.

The abstract states the dataset spans 'multiple redshifts,' but the training data is exclusively at z=0.5; redshift generalization is only evaluated, not represented in training. This presentation slightly oversells the dataset's coverage.

strengths: Well-motivated applied/systems contribution addressing a timely problem: automated, scalable mass reconstruction for the many low-to-moderate mass clusters expected from upcoming wide-field surveys, where expert-tuned methods like Lenstool/WSLAP+ do not scale.

DARKCLUSTERS-15K is a substantial community resource: 15,000 paired mass/photometry maps from two independent simulation frameworks (IllustrisTNG and SIMBA), with released generation code, simulated lensing observables, and careful train/test splits that keep all 25 views of a cluster in the same split, avoiding projection leakage.

Methodologically principled: the physics-guided diffusion approach (photometry-conditioned DDPM++ prior + DAPS posterior sampling with explicit weak/strong lensing forward models in the likelihood) is clearly formulated, moves beyond rigid light-traces-mass assumptions, and yields per-pixel uncertainties.

Strong experimental design: an ablation (Fig. 4) cleanly disentangles the contributions of the learned prior vs. lensing likelihood terms; uncertainty calibration is quantitatively verified (R²=0.99); held-out kappa RMSE at pixels without any photometry or lensing signal directly probes recovery of dark matter; Appendix C quantifies how far light-traces-mass holds (PCC ~0.58-0.65), grounding the claimed advantage over 1:1 LTM baselines.

Generalization is tested across lens redshifts (z_L in {0.2, 0.5, 1.0}) despite training only at z_L=0.5, and across simulation frameworks via the SIMBA test set; the method also outperforms both baselines on the out-of-framework SIMBA data.

Demonstration on real data (MACS 1206) against an expert Lenstool reconstruction, requiring no expert tuning and running in minutes, supports the practicality claim; code and dataset release supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Baseline coverage is limited: quantitative comparisons include only a re-implementation of Napier et al. and the authors' own UNet. MARS is dismissed for lack of a public implementation, and no quantitative comparison against expert-tuned tools (Lenstool, WSLAP+) on simulated data with known ground truth is provided, so the 'higher accuracy' claim rests on a narrow baseline set.

Evaluation is largely in-distribution: the lensing observations used at test time are generated by the same forward models used in the likelihood, and the calibration result (R²=0.99) is computed on held-out clusters from the same simulation and observation pipeline; real-observation mismatch (instrument noise beyond Gaussian shape noise, source redshift uncertainties, selection effects) is not characterized, making the calibration figure potentially optimistic.

Appendix B reveals that several inference hyperparameters (loss weights lambda_k, DAPS tau, learning rate) were chosen via parameter sweeps; while done on a validation subset, this partially softens the 'requires no expert tuning' claim, which is instead relative to per-cluster tuning in classical tools.

The strong-lensing photometric loss relies on a simplified Sérsic source model, and the weak-lensing term requires RBF interpolation of sparse, very noisy shear; the sensitivity of reconstruction quality to these modeling choices (e.g., misestimated Sérsic parameters, non-Gaussian shear noise) is not studied.

The MACS 1206 result is qualitative only (visual agreement of isolines); no quantitative metric or uncertainty comparison with the expert reconstruction is possible or attempted, and differences from prior-mismatch on real data are not analyzed.

Effective dataset diversity is narrower than the 15,000-sample count suggests: only 500 TNG clusters (25 projections each) and 60 SIMBA clusters underlie the data, and quantitative results in Table 2 are reported only at z_L=0.5, leaving redshift generalization supported by qualitative examples rather than metrics.
No limitations or societal-impact discussion, and the claim of possibly 'automating the detection of unobservable dark matter' in the introduction is not supported by any experiment.

strengths: Addresses a timely and well-motivated problem: scalable, fully automated reconstruction of cluster surface mass density for the hundreds of thousands of clusters expected from upcoming wide-field surveys, where current expert-tuned tools (Lenstool, WSLAP+) do not scale.

Two complementary contributions: (1) DarkClusters-15K, a large paired mass/photometry benchmark derived from IllustrisTNG and SIMBA with simulated weak/strong lensing observables, released with generation code for reproducibility; and (2) a physics-guided diffusion posterior sampling method (photometry-conditioned DDPM++ prior + lensing forward-model likelihoods within DAPS) that yields minute-scale reconstructions with per-pixel uncertainties.

Evaluation is reasonably thorough: ablation over photometry/strong/weak lensing inputs, comparison against three automated baselines (Kaiser-Squires, reimplemented Napier et al., UNet), held-out RMSE metrics at unconstrained pixels, and cross-framework generalization (TNG-trained model evaluated on SIMBA clusters and at multiple redshifts).
Uncertainty calibration is assessed quantitatively via a reliability diagram on held-out data, not just qualitatively - a rigor beyond many diffusion-for-inverse-problems papers.

Validation on real data (MACS 1206) against an expert Lenstool reconstruction is a convincing proof of concept: comparable multiple-image RMS scatter (0.56" vs 0.44") and 5.03% enclosed-mass error, within the ~10% spread reported between independent expert models, all without cluster-specific tuning.

Clear writing with a well-organized background section, honest comparison table of method capabilities (Table 1), and a useful supplemental analysis of the degree to which light-traces-mass holds in the data (PCC ~0.58-0.65), which substantiates the motivation for a learned mass-light prior.
weaknesses: The likelihood is only approximate in several ways - reduced shear g≈γ, RBF interpolation of sparse shear into a dense smoothed map, Sérsic source modeling in the photometric loss, and hand-specified loss weights λk (chosen via sweeps) - so the framing of the method as 'principled' posterior sampling with 'well-calibrated' uncertainties is somewhat stronger than what the approximate likelihood strictly supports.

Evidence for superiority over the strongest baseline is mixed: the UNet baseline actually achieves better held-out α RMSE than the proposed method on the TNG test set (0.411 vs 0.530), and on SIMBA the PSNR margin is modest (30.9 vs 29.6); the paper would benefit from analysis of when/why the diffusion method's added machinery matters, especially since UNet also does not use lensing data.

Comparison to the true state of the art is indirect: no quantitative comparison against Lenstool/WSLAP+ or MARS even on synthetic data (justified by expert tuning / unavailability, but expert-guided methods could still be run once on the test set to anchor performance), and the Napier et al. baseline is the authors' own reimplementation.

Dataset construction has potential leakage/correlation concerns: only 600 distinct clusters, expanded to 15,000 samples via 25 viewing directions per cluster; the paper should clarify that test clusters are fully disjoint from the 480 training clusters and discuss how intra-cluster projection correlation affects generalization claims.

Real-data validation is limited to a single cluster, uses only strong lensing (no real weak-lensing constraints), and involves a domain shift from simulated to real HST photometry that is not quantified; MACS 1206 is explicitly chosen as an unusually constraint-rich, clean cluster, so performance on typical clusters remains untested.

Training uses clusters at a single redshift (z=0.5) and a specific mass range and HST-like imaging setup; although the redshift generalization experiments are encouraging, robustness to different instruments, noise properties, and survey setups (e.g., ground-based weak lensing densities much lower than 30 galaxies/arcmin^2, or the non-standard 'kinematic' σ_w^2=0.03 regime) is unclear, and it is ambiguous which noise regime is used in the headline results of Table 2.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely important and timely problem: scalable, automated mass reconstruction of galaxy clusters for upcoming wide-field surveys (Euclid, LSST), where expert-tuned tools like Lenstool will not scale. The application motivation is well argued.

Two concrete contributions are released: DARKCLUSTERS-15K, the largest paired mass/photometry cluster dataset of its kind (spanning two independent simulation frameworks, multiple redshifts, and simulated lensing observables), plus code and a documented generation pipeline (Supplement A is thorough). This has clear value as a community benchmark.

The method is a sensible and mostly well-executed combination of existing components (DDPM++/EDM prior, DAPS posterior sampling, physical forward operators for strong/weak lensing). The conditioning of the prior on photometry rather than assuming a rigid light-traces-mass relation is a well-motivated design choice, and Appendix D quantitatively supports it.

The evaluation is reasonably comprehensive: an ablation of photometry/strong/weak-lensing inputs, calibration of uncertainties via reliability diagrams, comparisons across three automated baselines, tests of generalization to unseen redshifts and to an entirely different simulation (SIMBA), and an end-to-end demonstration on real HST data (MACS 1206) where the reconstruction matches an expert Lenstool solution in morphology, critical-curve structure, multiple-image RMS (0.56" vs 0.44"), and enclosed mass (~5% error vs the ~10% spread between independent expert models).
Practicality claims (minutes per cluster, no per-cluster tuning, single-GPU training) are credible and well supported.

The paper is clearly written, with a well-structured background section that makes it accessible to a non-specialist vision audience, and limitations of baselines are described fairly rather than strawmanned.
weaknesses: The framing as a 'principled' posterior is overstated. The likelihood is replaced by a weighted sum of heuristic loss terms (Eq. 10) with hand-tuned weights λk, and weak-lensing data are RBF-smoothed into a dense pseudo-observation rather than modeled at their native sparse positions. This makes the output an approximate, heuristic-guided sample; the reported calibration is marginal-only and could hide per-pixel miscalibration. The paper would benefit from more caution in its uncertainty claims.

The learned prior is trained exclusively on TNG300-1 clusters at zL = 0.5. Reconstructions therefore inherit simulation-specific baryonic physics and (potentially) dataset biases; while the SIMBA transfer test is a good sanity check, the paper does not analyze failure modes when real clusters deviate from the simulation prior (e.g., merging systems, line-of-sight structures, or external convergence — MACS 1206 was explicitly chosen because it lacks these).

The real-data demonstration uses strong lensing only; weak lensing, a headline component of the method, is not exercised on real data, and no weak-lensing comparison (e.g., against the observed shear profile of MACS 1206) is provided.

Baseline coverage is limited. The strongest expert-guided tools (Lenstool, WSLAP+) and MARS are not run on the mock benchmark (justified by availability/tuning cost, but a mock-set Lenstool or hybrid-lenstool run on a subset would substantially strengthen the comparison). Table 2 also reports only medians over 100 clusters with no spread or significance tests, and held-out RMSE metrics favor methods with any prior on cluster morphology.

Statistical independence in the dataset is weaker than the sample counts suggest: 25 projections of the same 3D cluster are highly correlated, and the 20 test clusters reused across three redshifts mean the zL-generalization test partially re-evaluates the same objects. The effective diversity is ~600 clusters, and potential cross-projection information leakage (same substructure at different viewing angles) is not discussed.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: 'achieves higher accuracy' than expert tools is only established against reimplementations and automated baselines on synthetic data; the assertion that the method 'could automate the detection of unobservable dark matter' is speculative.
Only 20 posterior samples are used for mean/std/calibration estimates; no convergence analysis of the sampler is given, and computational cost of the 20-sample uncertainty estimates is not reported.

strengths: Significant dual contribution: DARKCLUSTERS-15K (15,000 mock cluster observations with paired mass/photometry from two independent simulations) is the largest benchmark of its kind, and the diffusion-based reconstruction method is the first to combine a data-driven score prior with weak-lensing, strong-lensing, and photometry at cluster scale.

The method is well-motivated physically: factorizing a photometry-conditioned diffusion prior from physics-based lensing likelihoods (DAPS-style posterior sampling) is a principled design, and the ablation in Section 6.2 cleanly disentangles the contribution of each input, showing photometry alone overshoots mass and lensing constraints correct it.
Uncertainty quantification is treated seriously, with a reliability diagram showing calibrated marginal coverage on held-out data rather than anecdotal error bars.

Evidence of generalization is reasonably thorough: testing on held-out clusters at different redshifts (zL = 0.2–1.0) and on the entirely different SIMBA simulation framework, plus a real-data proof of concept on MACS 1206 that matches expert-tuned reconstructions (0.56" vs 0.44" RMS scatter; 5% enclosed-mass error, comparable to the ~10% spread among expert models).

Comparisons to three automated baselines (Kaiser-Squires, a reimplementation of Napier et al., and a UNet) with quantitative and qualitative analysis, and the released dataset/code support reproducibility. The supplemental (mass/light PCC analysis in App. D) honestly quantifies when the light-traces-mass assumption breaks.
Clear writing, well-structured motivation connecting method design to the needs of upcoming wide-field surveys (Euclid/LSST-scale cluster counts).
weaknesses: The 'no expert tuning' claim is somewhat overstated: loss weights λk, DAPS parameters τ, and learning rate were chosen via parameter sweeps on a validation set (App. C). While automated sweeps are more scalable than cluster-specific expert modeling, the sensitivity of results to these hyperparameters is not characterized.

Only one real cluster (MACS 1206) is evaluated, and it was explicitly chosen because it is unusually rich in strong-lensing constraints and free of external convergence/shear. The sim-to-real gap on typical clusters with sparser data remains untested, despite this being the paper's core motivation.

The diffusion prior is trained exclusively on TNG clusters at zL = 0.5; generalization to zL = 0.2/1.0 and SIMBA is shown empirically, but a prior mismatch across redshift or simulation physics (e.g., baryonic feedback differences between TNG and SIMBA) could bias the posterior in ways PSNR/SSIM on mocks cannot fully reveal.

Several physics approximations are made without sensitivity analysis: reduced shear g ≈ γ in the weak regime, lossy RBF interpolation of sparse shear, a Sérsic source model in the photometric loss, and unknown source positions estimated by averaging. How these affect the accuracy of the claimed posterior is not quantified.

Posterior validity rests on heuristic diffusion posterior sampling (DAPS with hand-weighted, heuristically scaled likelihood terms); calibration is demonstrated only on in-distribution mock data, and 20 posterior samples is a small budget for the coverage claims.

The UNet baseline difference conflates two factors: access to lensing data and the diffusion-vs-regression architecture. A cleaner attribution of gains would help. Similarly, comparison against expert tools (Lenstool, WSLAP+) is necessarily qualitative since they were not run, and the Napier et al. method was reimplemented rather than run with its original calibration.

Evaluation metrics (PSNR/SSIM/PCC on κ maps) are standard but may not reflect the astrophysical quantities of actual interest (e.g., subhalo mass function, mass-profile slopes relevant to time-delay cosmology); a domain-expert-oriented metric would strengthen the case for downstream scientific utility.
